problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

activity_context.topic_title: Projecting Vectors Onto Subspaces in Euclidean Spaces (Arbitrary Bases): Applications

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto the Solution Space of a Linear System
examples.problem:
Given the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system.
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/043050d4ab229a40aef87d4a404f5af2337a36d1ba54926dcb9a214fdad5e245.png)
examples.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2,$ and $x_3$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get $x_1 = 2x_2-3x_3.$ Therefore, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/8aac548229fb8312eefaed282dd27daadf560b17009f163d568ca1edda949a69.png)

Consequently, 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/b241f88f83f96ef2f393b7450e5933831b300b98522b16b02208298db1b4ea91.png)
is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we let $A$ be a matrix whose columns equal the elements of $\mathcal B,$ and we find the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & -6 \\ -6 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 8 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
feedback.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}6 & 6 \\ 6 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$   

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 2+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{12}} \\  & =\frac{12}{2\sqrt{42}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}})≈{22.21}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.
